name: Zane Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a water truck at a large mine, keeping the roads damp enough that the haul crews can see. At 43 I am still a junior operator, and I have to ask which sections take water first when the wind turns. I like a job with a visible result: the dust settles and another driver gets home with clean sight. My wife Leah works at a bakery, and our two children are in school. My mine wage is high for this work, we have a mortgage, and we have saved over six months of expenses by keeping our spending plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a small saving in paperwork is no reason to change the water run. The road is dusty or it isn't, and I still need to see it before I spray. I don't use AI tools; I take the route sheet and talk to the haul drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my truck shifts and Leah's bakery hours to carry on. Our savings would cover more than six months of bills if something ordinary went wrong, and the mortgage is manageable on current pay. I still count every school expense, because a good wage can disappear faster than a family learns to spend less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the morning water route and ask the lead driver where the wind pushed dust overnight. Leah and I would continue our usual mortgage payment and leave the savings account for a real emergency. In the first year I'd work the same shifts and check the bakery rota before promising the children an extra trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job in this picture. The little office change doesn't reach the road, and the household budget is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the wind change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bend near the upper haul road can turn white with dust before lunch. If I miss it, the truck behind me is driving nearly blind, so I ask the driver who passed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the bakery rota before a trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah has early shifts and sometimes a weekend order. We won't buy tickets on the assumption that she can take a day off.

say: I would say **paperwork savings** do not change the road’s need for water.
I use a **route and reports**, not AI tools.
think: I expect my shifts and Leah’s **bakery hours** to hold.
Our **savings and wages** cover the mortgage and ordinary school costs.
do: Keep the morning **water route** and ask drivers about overnight dust.
Continue usual **mortgage payments** and check Leah’s rota before trips.
feel: **Calm** about work and the household budget.

fieldNote: Zane’s physical safety task and strong savings support a **calm** mild-scenario response.

steps.text: Keep the morning water route and check dusty sections with haul drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine can make buying and planning faster, but the road still needs someone watching it. If a new schedule says one water run is enough, I want the supervisor to drive the route before agreeing. Good planning is useful only when drivers can see the bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A junior operator can lose hours when a planner decides the truck should cover more ground in less time. Leah's bakery work seems less touched by office AI, yet my higher mine wage is what makes the mortgage comfortable. There are plenty of other mines around, but a new place might pay less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to ride the first route under any new schedule and mark the dusty bends with me. I'd keep the current shifts while the plan is tested. If mine hours fall in the first year, I'd apply to two nearby pits and stop the extra holiday we talked about for summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the plan and anxious about an hours cut. I can look for another job, but I don't want to put the children's routine through a move for a bad spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The upper bend where the wind pushes dust back across the road. I would ask her to watch one loaded truck pass there before signing a shorter route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the planning system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen to an explanation, but I don't want to run it myself yet. The supervisor can show me a proven route; I need to see the dust with my eyes.

say: I would say **faster planning** still needs a road check before water runs shrink.
I want the supervisor to **drive the route** before accepting a new schedule.
think: My **junior hours** could fall even while the truck remains useful.
Another mine is possible, but losing my **higher wage** would tighten the mortgage.
do: Ride the new **water route** with a supervisor and mark dusty bends.
Keep current shifts while the **plan is tested**.
Apply to nearby pits and cancel the **summer holiday** if hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, despite local job options.
S1.quote: Good planning is useful only when drivers can see the bend.
fieldNote: Zane is willing to observe a new route but wants **physical proof** before hours change.
His caution comes from the mortgage and children, though **nearby pits** offer alternatives.

steps.text: Keep driving the water truck during the route trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family that full thinking AI comes by 2028, and trucks able to do hands-on work as well as us come around 2031. The office may change first, but that doesn't make my water truck safe after the second date. I want the mine to tell every driver what paid work will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not quick with new technology, and two years is not much time to learn a different trade. At 48 in 2031 I could lose my higher mine wage while our children still need us and the mortgage is running. The savings are solid but won't last through years without a wage, and Leah's bakery pay cannot carry everything alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine for a written timetable for driver numbers and the robot fleet. I'd keep taking the water run and add part of each pay packet to the mortgage reserve. In 2029 I'd apply for water-truck jobs at other nearby mines and ask about a paid machine-servicing apprenticeship if the wage covers our bills. If robots replace the truck in 2031, I'd take another paid driving job while considering the apprenticeship, not sit at home waiting for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the short notice, but I know what call to make first. I keep picturing the mortgage letter arriving after my last mine pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the other mines avoid robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. A nearby water truck job could keep the mortgage paid while I learn whether servicing is a real route, not a lifetime guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with the children if shifts changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah's sister lives close and has helped with pickup before. I would ask her only for a short bridge, because she has her own work and home.

say: I would explain **2028 office AI** and capable trucks around **2031** as separate risks.
I want a written count of **paid driver jobs** after robots arrive.
think: My slow technology learning makes a **short trade switch** hard.
At 48, losing my higher wage would threaten **mortgage payments** beyond our savings.
do: Ask the mine for **driver and robot dates**.
Keep the water run and add wages to a **mortgage reserve**.
Apply in 2029 for **nearby driving work** and ask about paid servicing.
feel: **Frightened** by the short notice, with a first call in mind.
S2.quote: A nearby water truck job could keep the mortgage paid while I learn whether servicing is a real route, not a lifetime guarantee.
fieldNote: He knows the **2031 robot date** threatens his hands-on truck work after earlier office changes.
He asks about a paid apprenticeship but cannot afford **unpaid learning** while children and mortgage depend on wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the mine time to offer proper apprenticeships instead of just telling people to adapt. Thinking AI arrives around 2031, and trucks that can do our work arrive around 2034. If the mine expects a smaller driver crew, it should say so while people can still earn and learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when the office changes and 51 when the robot trucks arrive. Our children will be older, but we may still need to help them, and the mortgage isn't guaranteed to be gone. I could manage a paid apprenticeship over several years if the work is taught beside a mechanic, not dumped on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the workshop foreman whether the mine will sponsor a paid servicing apprenticeship and what wages it pays in year one. If the terms work, I'd enrol while keeping my water-truck shifts where possible. In 2032 I'd check the driver rota and apply to other nearby mines if our hours are already falling. Before 2034 I'd choose a paid servicing place or a paid driving offer based on actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to breathe with five years. I don't want the mine to spend four years discussing a course nobody can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tyres, brakes and the water pump I already hear every day. I'd learn from a mechanic with a tool in hand before I trusted myself with a remote screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family support the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah would, if the first-year wage covered the mortgage and regular bills. We would check the numbers together before I signed anything.

Drivers need the **2034 robot plan** while they can still earn and learn.

I could learn servicing beside a **mechanic**, given paid time.
do: Ask the foreman about a **paid servicing apprenticeship**.
Enrol if wages cover bills while **keeping truck shifts** where possible.
Check 2032 rosters and apply to **nearby mines** if hours fall.
feel: More **breathing room**, provided the employer acts early.

fieldNote: Zane’s willingness to change depends on **paid apprenticeship terms** and hands-on teaching.

steps.text: Enrol in machine servicing if the apprenticeship wage covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a decade is enough for an honest plan, if managers start now. Thinking AI reaches the office in 2036 and capable robot trucks arrive around 2039. I'd ask for one yearly meeting on driver numbers and apprenticeships instead of a last-minute notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 at the first date and 56 at the robot date. Our children should be grown by then, so the bus passes and school shoes won't be monthly costs, but the mortgage could still be there. I don't know what pension we will have and I expect to keep earning, perhaps at another mine if this one cuts drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the water route and ask at my annual review for the mine's driver and apprenticeship numbers. Leah and I would make an extra mortgage payment each quarter from my higher wage if ordinary bills allow, leaving the emergency savings intact. In 2037 I'd ask the workshop foreman about paid service work, and I'd apply to a nearby mine if the local driver openings dried up. Before 2039 we'd check the pension statement, but I wouldn't leave paid work without a replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, not crushed, with that much time. Ten years gives me room to make careful moves without pretending retirement is already paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if servicing uses a lot of software by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see the job and whether I could learn it beside someone. I won't say yes merely because the title sounds practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them a good wage comes from learning a skill and keeping it useful. I wouldn't promise them the water-truck seat will be there for their turn.

A decade is useful only if managers **start planning now**.

I expect **continued paid work**, not an assumed pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because a capable truck could take my run by 2031, before I had learned another paid trade. A written driver plan and a servicing apprenticeship with a first-year wage would help. Leah and I can bridge a few months with savings, not an endless gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a mine will pay someone to teach the new apprentice rather than hand over a manual. I learn beside a person, and a wage without proper teaching would still leave me unready. A machine manual cannot show me what a mechanic hears in a failing pump.

headlineQuote: A machine manual cannot show me what a mechanic hears in a failing pump.
portrait: Zane is a **43-year-old junior water-truck driver** who keeps dusty mine roads visible.
His **higher wage and savings** support Leah, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He avoids AI tools and prefers **hands-on teaching** before taking a risk on unfamiliar equipment.
He would keep paid driving, seek a **servicing apprenticeship** and reduce the mortgage over a longer warning.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because capable trucks arrive around 2031 before he can comfortably learn another trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **written driver plan** and a paid servicing apprenticeship with patient instruction would help him replace wages.
